rouse

/rouz/ — rhymes with 'house' and 'mouse' · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To rouse someone is to wake them up or stir them into action or alertness.

The smell of pancakes finally roused the campers from their sleeping bags.

Example

The coach's passionate halftime speech roused the team from their discouraged silence, and they returned to the court with renewed determination.

Rouse is more precise than just 'wake' because it captures not only waking but stirring someone into alertness and action. The word carries the sense of energy and purpose—something actively moving a person from inactivity into engagement. That's what rouse names exactly.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

wake: To wake someone is simply to bring them out of sleep — the plain fact of leaving sleep, nothing more. To rouse goes further: it wakes a person and stirs them into alertness or action, the way a fire alarm sends a whole dorm scrambling into the hall.

awaken: To awaken someone is to bring them out of sleep gently and gradually — first light easing a sleeper toward morning. Rouse is more forceful: to rouse someone is to pull them from sleep or stillness into full alertness, often pushing them straight into action.

prod: To prod someone is to keep nudging or nagging them toward a task they are avoiding — pressure applied to a person who is already awake. To rouse is to move someone out of sleep or stillness in the first place, bringing them to alertness before any task begins.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

lull: soothe someone toward sleep or calm

sedate: make someone calm, quiet, and slow

Where it sits · how forcefully stillness turns to action — rest → stir → rouse → galvanize

rest vs. rouse: Rest sits at the opposite end of the scale from rouse: resting means settling into stillness, while rousing means being pulled out of stillness into alertness.

stir vs. rouse: Stir is weaker than rouse; to stir is to barely begin moving, while to rouse someone is to bring them fully awake or push them into real action.

galvanize vs. rouse: Galvanize is stronger than rouse — rousing gets people up and moving, but galvanizing jolts them into sudden, energized action, like an electric shock.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — rouse

Root — rouse: to shake up, start into motion (originally a hawk shaking its feathers) (Middle English, possibly via Anglo-French)

Put it together

Put it together: Rouse is a single root that entered English as a hawking term for a bird shaking its feathers awake — that idea of shaking someone out of sleep or stillness and into action still sits at the heart of the word.

Use the root in a new word: arouse

Use the root in a new word: arouse: The mystery novel aroused everyone's curiosity, just as a good campfire story can rouse a sleepy group to full attention — arouse is simply rouse with an added prefix.

Word Choice

neutral

Use rouse when someone or something actively wakes or stirs another person into alertness or action. A smell rouses you from sleep. A speech rouses a crowd to action. A sound rouses you from deep thought. 'Wake' is simpler and works for plain falling asleep; 'rouse' is more precise when energy, purpose, or stirring is involved.
